hints: Focus on what kind of structure silicon dioxide has, giant covalent like diamond, not ionic or simple molecular.
Remember that conduction in the liquid state needs mobile charged particles, either ions or delocalised electrons.
Think about whether very strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice can be broken by water to allow dissolving.
walkthrough:
**Identify the structure of silicon dioxide**

Think of $\text{SiO}_2$ as sand or quartz. It has a giant covalent lattice with each Si bonded to four O atoms in a strong 3D network.

Structure type:
$$\text{SiO}_2 = \text{giant covalent (macromolecular)}$$

**Decide on electrical conductivity in liquid state**

For a liquid to conduct, it needs mobile ions or mobile electrons. $\text{SiO}_2$ has no ions at all and all electrons are locked in covalent bonds, even when molten.

Rule:
$$\text{no mobile ions, no delocalised electrons} \rightarrow \text{non-conductor}$$

**Decide on solubility in water**

Water cannot break the very strong Si-O covalent bonds in the giant lattice. So silicon dioxide does not dissolve, unlike simple covalent oxides such as $\text{SO}_2$.

Conclusion: non-conductor and insoluble, which matches the correct row.

options.A: Correct. Giant covalent $\text{SiO}_2$ has no mobile ions or free electrons, so it is a non-conductor even as a liquid. Its strong lattice is not broken by water, so it is insoluble.
options.B: Incorrect. While non-conductor is right, soluble is wrong. Students may confuse $\text{SiO}_2$ with acidic simple oxides like $\text{CO}_2$ or $\text{SO}_2$ which do dissolve to form acids.
options.C: Incorrect. While insoluble is right, conductor is wrong. Students may think that because it melts, charged particles become free to move as in ionic compounds, but $\text{SiO}_2$ contains no ions.
options.D: Incorrect on both counts. Students may treat silicon dioxide as if it were an ionic oxide like $\text{MgO}$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, which conduct when molten and are soluble or reactive with water.
